05-001.r: Liquid (e.g. kerosene) → fixed volume, no fixed shape; solid (carbon steel) → fixed shape and volume; gas (krypton) → neither.

05-002.r: Only statement 2 is true: stretching of a coil depends on shear modulus. Statement 1 false: steel's Young's modulus is much greater than rubber's.

05-003.r: Bulk modulus (K = stress/strain) of a perfectly rigid body is infinite: its volume never changes (ΔV = 0) under any pressure.

05-004.r: Both true: coefficients of linear expansion (α = ΔL/LΔT) and volume expansion (γ) have dimension K⁻¹ (per unit change in temperature).

05-005.r: Same material and load: elongation ∝ length ÷ (diameter)² → the 3 m long, 1.5 mm thick wire stretches most.

05-006.r: Raindrops are spherical due to surface tension: a liquid drop takes the least surface area, and a sphere has the least area for its volume.

05-010.r: Oil spreads on water because oil's surface tension is less than water's; water's stronger surface tension pulls the oil in all directions.

05-011.r: Kerosene floats on water because its density is less than that of water.
05-011.t: Floating depends on density; spreading of oil on water depends on surface tension.

05-012.r: Pressure inside a soap bubble is more than atmospheric pressure; soap reduces the surface tension of water.

05-013.r: Excess pressure in a soap bubble ∝ 1/radius: joined by a tube, air flows from the small to the big bubble → small shrinks, big grows.

05-014.r: Rising hydrogen balloon → outside air pressure falls while inside pressure stays nearly constant → balloon increases in size.

05-015.r: Charging a soap bubble increases its radius: the like charges spread over the surface and repel each other.

05-016.r: Without capillarity, kerosene lamp wicks, blotting paper and tall trees would fail (1, 3, 4); drinking through a straw does not depend on capillarity.

05-017.r: Water rising from roots to leaves is not due to capillarity alone (also transpiration and cohesion); blotting ink, rising groundwater, water spreading on cotton are capillarity.

05-018.r: Kerosene rises in a stove or lamp wick due to surface tension: the wick's many fine holes act as capillaries.

05-019.r: Capillary rise is proportional to surface tension: a liquid with more surface tension than water rises higher.

05-020.r: An air bubble rising from a lake bottom grows bigger: the water pressure on it falls as depth decreases.

05-021.r: Fountain pens leak in planes (high altitude): outside air pressure is low, so the higher-pressure ink flows out.

05-022.r: Hydraulic brakes, press and elevator → Pascal's law: pressure on a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

05-023.r: Sudden fall in barometer reading → stormy weather (atmospheric pressure drops quickly as a storm begins).

05-024.r: Torricelli's law: velocity of efflux grows with the depth (h) of the hole, so the deepest hole (hole 1) throws water farthest.

05-025.r: Streamlined flow in a pipe: liquid layers are slowest near the pipe wall and speed up towards the axis.

05-026.r: Viscosity of a liquid decreases as temperature rises (water: 1.308 mPa·s at 10°C, 0.5471 at 50°C).

05-027.r: Viscosity = a fluid's resistance to flow; among water, air, blood and honey, honey has the highest.

05-028.r: Most viscous among alcohol, water, honey and gasoline → honey (viscosity ≈ 'thickness' of a liquid).

05-029.r: A false: glycerin's (any liquid's) viscosity decreases with rising temperature. R true: heat increases the kinetic energy of molecules.

05-030.r: Density depends on mass and volume (density = mass/volume), so adding more of a substance does not change its density.

05-031.r: Lake surface freezes but the bottom stays liquid because water has maximum density (least volume) at 4°C.

05-032.r: Aquatic animals survive frozen lakes: water is densest at 4°C, so a liquid layer at 4°C stays below the ice (winter stratification).

05-034.r: Water heated from 0°C to 10°C: volume first decreases (till 4°C, maximum density), then increases like other liquids.

05-035.r: Water cooled from 9°C to 3°C: volume first decreases (till 4°C, maximum density) and then increases.

05-036.r: Water is densest (least volume) at 4°C; between 0°C and 4°C it contracts on heating: anomalous expansion of water.

05-038.t: 273 K = 0°C; maximum density is at 4°C = 277 K.

05-039.r: Avogadro's law: at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain an equal number of molecules.

05-040.r: Gases liquefy at low temperature and high pressure: pressure pushes molecules together, cooling lowers their kinetic energy.

05-041.r: Distance between CO2 molecules in a container increases when its volume is increased or some gas leaks; it decreases with more pressure or more gas.

05-042.r: Gas law: at fixed pressure volume ∝ kelvin temperature; gas at 27°C squeezed to half volume must double its kelvin temperature → three hundred twenty-seven °C.

05-043.r: Iron floats on mercury but sinks in water: iron is denser than water but less dense than mercury. A true; R (iron's specific gravity > mercury's) false.

05-045.r: Relative density of water = 1; above 1 sinks, below 1 floats. A needle is denser than water and sinks; a ship's effective density (m/v) is less, so it floats.

05-046.r: An iron needle can float on water due to surface tension, whose upward force balances the needle's weight.

05-047.r: A bucket feels heavier once out of water: in water, upthrust (Archimedes' principle) reduces apparent weight by the weight of water displaced.

05-048.r: 200 g of water in a weightless balloon weighs zero in water: weight − upthrust = 200 − 200 = 0.

05-049.r: Clouds float because of their low density: the buoyant force of the surrounding air balances their weight.

05-050.r: Ice is about 9/10 as dense as water; an iceberg floating in the denser sea keeps about 1/8 to 1/9 of itself above the surface.

05-051.r: Floating ice displaces water equal to its own weight (Archimedes' principle), so when it melts the water level stays the same.

05-053.r: A body floating in 4°C water (maximum density) sinks when the water reaches 100°C (lowest density).

05-054.r: Swimming is easier in the sea: dissolved salts raise water's density and upthrust.

05-055.r: A body weighs most in hydrogen: the lightest gas gives the least upthrust (buoyant force).

05-056.r: A ship entering the sea from a river rises a little: salty sea water is denser than river water.

06-001.r: Moon is non-luminous (it only reflects sunlight); candle flame, electric lamp and the Sun are luminous (give their own light).

06-002.r: Photon energy E = hc/λ: shorter wavelength → more energy per quantum, so 200–280 nm (ultraviolet) is the most energetic option.

06-003.r: Visible light = 400–700 nm; infrared above 700 nm; ultraviolet below 400 nm.

06-004.r: Visible light ≈ 380–700 nm (3800–7000 Å), between infrared and ultraviolet; best option 390–780 nm (variant: 3900–7600 Å).

06-006.r: The eye is most sensitive to yellowish-green light of about 5550 Å (555 nm); nearest option 5500 Å.

06-007.r: The eye is most sensitive to colours between yellow and green (wavelengths 530–570 nm).

06-008.r: False: eye most sensitive to red; it peaks at yellowish-green (555 nm). Ear most sensitive near 1000 Hz; persistence of hearing 1/10 s, of vision 1/16 s.

06-009.r: Light has a dual nature: it behaves both as a wave and as a particle (black body radiation and photoelectric effect need the particle model).

06-010.r: Light appears to travel in a straight line because its wavelength is very small.

06-011.r: Light is fastest: about 3 lakh km/s in vacuum (2 lakh km/s in glass); sound travels 343 m/s in air and not at all in vacuum.

06-014.r: Speed of light in air depends on its optical density (refractive index), which changes with air's temperature, pressure and humidity, not its physical density.
06-014.c: The book gives no single answer (*): by its explanation both pressure and temperature affect it, so no one option is complete.

06-015.r: Light is faster in air than in water (statement I correct); water's refractive index is higher than air's (statement II wrong).

06-016.r: Light is fastest in vacuum (c ≈ 3 lakh km/s); it slows in optically denser media like water and glass and is slowest in diamond.

06-018.r: Higher refractive index → lower speed of light; among glass, vacuum, water and air, light is slowest in glass.

06-019.r: Sunlight takes about 499 seconds (≈ 8.3 minutes) to reach Earth; answer options: 8.5 minutes or 'about 8 minutes'.

06-022.r: Nothing travels faster than light; light beats cosmic rays, electrons and supersonic waves and can travel through vacuum (sound cannot).

06-023.r: When light passes from one medium to another, frequency stays the same; velocity and wavelength change (air to glass).

06-026.r: Denser → rarer medium: light speeds up and bends away from the normal; rarer → denser: it slows down and bends towards the normal.

06-027.r: Glittering colours of thin soap foam → total reflection and interference of light reflected from the film's outer and inner surfaces.

06-028.r: Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium at more than the critical angle → possible from diamond to glass.

06-029.r: A cut diamond shines brilliantly due to total internal reflection; its critical angle is low, about 24.4 degrees.

06-030.r: Diamond looks lustrous due to total internal reflection: very high refractive index → very low critical angle → light reflects many times inside.

06-032.r: Diamond sparkles more than glass of the same shape (A true) because its refractive index is higher (2.42 vs glass 1.51); R ('less than glass') false.

06-033.r: Optical fibre (thin strand of glass/silica or plastic) works on total internal reflection.

06-036.r: Fibre-optic communication sends information as pulses of light (light waves) through optical fibre.

06-037.r: Optical fibre: total internal reflection, very low power use, no radio-frequency interference (1, 2, 3 true). Statement 4 false: Sterlite-Tech (from 2000), not Reliance, makes it.

06-038.r: Endoscope (to view inside the stomach and body cavities) works on total internal reflection in a bundle of optical fibres.

06-040.r: Mirage → refraction and total internal reflection of light through air layers of different densities (hot desert ground).

06-043.r: Fresh snow reflects the most sunlight (about 80–85%); a surface's power to reflect light is called albedo (Latin: 'whiteness').

06-044.r: Holography → technique to produce a three-dimensional image of an object (used to preserve transcripts, microfiche, three-dimensional films).

06-046.r: Roster (raster) scan → an electron gun's beam builds the image on a phosphor-coated CRT (Cathode Ray Tube) screen.

06-047.r: Raman effect → light passing through any transparent medium; a small fraction emerges in directions other than the incident beam (scattering).

06-048.r: A CD player reproduces sound using a laser beam reflected from the bright surface of the disc.

06-049.r: Rainbow colours on a CD in sunlight → reflection and diffraction (a CD is polycarbonate plastic with a thin aluminium layer).

06-050.r: True: 3 (radio waves from rapidly oscillating currents), 4 (police use Doppler effect). False: shorter wavelengths scatter more; light in water ≈ 0.75, not 0.95, of vacuum speed.

06-051.r: Films project 24 frames per second (A true), but an image persists on the retina about 1/16 s, not 0.1 s (R false).

06-052.r: Retina → photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) turn light into neural impulses, sent by the optic nerve to the brain.

06-053.r: Image on the retina is real, inverted and smaller than the object; the brain, from experience, lets us see it upright.

06-055.r: Two eyes give stereoscopic vision: two slightly different images combine into a three-dimensional picture, improving depth and distance perception.

06-056.r: Looking directly at the Sun during a solar eclipse can cause permanent eye damage (retinal burn) from its ultraviolet (UV) rays.

06-057.r: A star's colour shows its temperature: blue = high temperature (young star), red = low temperature.

06-058.r: Diffusion (scattering) of sunlight in the atmosphere is caused by dust particles (and air molecules).

06-060.r: Colour of light is decided by its wavelength: red has the longest, violet the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum.
06-060.h: VIBGYOR: wavelength grows from Violet to Red.
